title: After the Fire, Before a Lease
displayTitle: After the Fire, Before a Lease
subtitle: For renters displaced by Los Angeles's January 2025 fires, finding somewhere to stay left another question: how long could they afford to remain?
excerpt: For renters displaced by Los Angeles's January 2025 fires, finding somewhere to stay left another question: how long could they afford to remain?

content.alt: Aerial view of fire-damaged homes and businesses in Altadena
content.caption: Fire-damaged homes and businesses along Lake Street in Altadena. Added to this article on September 26, 2026; the photograph’s capture date has not been confirmed.

content.text: Even before the Eaton fire, Chevondolyn could no longer afford her apartment in Santa Clarita. This mother of two children moved in with relatives. The January fire affected the community she had recently returned to. In an August 2025 report, Union Station Homeless Services described how she lost everything after experiencing financial hardship.

Between February 1 and March 30, 2025, USC researchers conducted a survey of 1,360 Los Angeles County residents. Among evacuees who were already experiencing housing insecurity before the fires, 22 percent had not returned home at the time of the survey, compared to 15 percent of those who had stable housing.

A family may need a certain number of bedrooms, a location that makes it easy to commute to work, or a place from which children can continue attending school. Moving further away changes the support network available for childcare. Living with relatives offers immediate refuge, but leaves the long-term situation uncertain.

While helping refugee families find housing in Long Beach, I had to keep track of apartment bedrooms, income limits, deposits and credit requirements. I called properties to verify their conditions and determine if each option was suitable for the families.

This experience made me cautious about considering a list of available properties as a list of homes that people can actually move into. A family may be able to pay the monthly rent, but need help with the deposit. Or, an apartment fits the budget, but doesn't have enough space for the entire family.

In California, the housing department tried to do this type of matching after the fires. In July, it announced that 141 properties — responding to its survey of state-funded housing in Los Angeles County — had 723 vacant units in June. The housing department provided the list to the county to help displaced residents find housing. However, residents had to meet established eligibility criteria.

content.alt: Workers at the timber frame of a home under construction on Palm Street in Altadena
content.caption: A home under construction on Palm Street in Altadena, April 30, 2026.

content.text: The count of vacant units did not indicate how many households qualified, how many applied or how many moved in.

Emergency accommodation helped some of the survivors begin their search for housing. Airbnb.org coordinated with the 211 LA service to manage free stays for fire victims. In a Jan. 29 update, Airbnb announced that more than 17,000 people had booked temporary accommodations through its response program. The announcement also mentioned allocating funds to cover additional nights and extensions of stay for those who lost their homes.

In July, LAist reporters — in an article republished by KQED — noted that the organization 211 LA was working with more than 3,000 households affected by the fires, mostly renters. Maribel Marin, executive director of 211 LA, indicated that users faced much higher rents for similar homes. The report also cites data from the organization that reveals that more than 100 families were living in vehicles. These figures referred only to people within their care network, and not to the total number of displaced families in the county.

Union Station Homeless Services described a program for fire victims that covers security deposits, back rent, basic furniture and motel vouchers; In addition, it offers assistance for paying rent to those households that need it for a period of more than one month. It was noted that the program was designed to reduce the barriers faced by people who do not qualify for accessing traditional assistance.

content.caption: An image accompanying USHS’s account of its Eaton Fire Housing Assistance Program. The source does not identify the people pictured.

content.text: Door of Hope combined housing assistance with guidance on how to access other resources. In March, the Pasadena Community Foundation announced that the organization was providing support to families moving into new apartments, filing paperwork with FEMA and insurance companies, and covering expenses not covered by other sources of aid. Funds also supported a disaster case manager, who could assist families with health care, therapy and job search issues.
Will Chevondolyn and other displaced tenants be able to afford to stay once assistance ends?

reportingNote: The sources were first published between January and August 2025. The two USHS pages show later updates dated October 21, 2025; their current wording has not been checked against a summer 2025 archived version. Chevondolyn's experience comes from USHS's published account, not an interview conducted for The Margins. My housing-search observations come from work with refugee families in Long Beach.
